listening.title: A morning at the community garden
listening.intro: You will hear a student, Farah, telling her class about a morning she spent helping at a community garden. Answer questions 1 to 6. You will hear the recording twice.

script.text: Good morning, everyone. Last month my aunt asked me to help at the community garden near her block in Tampines. To be honest, I only agreed because she promised me lunch afterwards. I imagined a few flower pots along a corridor. I was wrong. The garden was the size of two basketball courts, hidden behind a multi-storey car park, and there were already about twenty people working when we arrived at half past seven.

A retired bus driver called Mr Goh was in charge. He did not ask what I was good at. He simply handed me a pair of gloves and pointed at a pile of compost. For the first hour I carried buckets of it to the vegetable beds. It smelt terrible, my arms ached, and I kept checking my watch.

Things changed when Mr Goh showed me the lady's fingers. He explained that if you leave them on the plant for even two days too long, they turn hard and nobody can eat them. So someone has to check every plant, every morning. I had always thought vegetables just appeared in the supermarket. Suddenly I understood how much patience was behind one plate of food.

After that I stopped looking at my watch. I harvested a whole basket myself, and Mr Goh let me weigh it: almost three kilograms. The vegetables are not sold. Every Saturday the volunteers pack them into bags and leave them at the lift lobbies for elderly residents who live alone.

What surprised me most was not the garden. It was the people. Nobody was paid, nobody was forced, and yet they turned up at sunrise every week. I went for a free lunch. I have now been back three times, and my aunt has stopped offering to pay for the food.

listening.title: Planning the class outing
listening.intro: You will hear two classmates, Priya and Wei Jie, planning a class outing for the end of term. Answer questions 1 to 7. You will hear the recording twice.

script.text: Wei Jie, Mrs Tan wants our plan for the class outing by Friday. Have you looked at the four ideas the class voted for?
I have. Shall we start with the kayaking at the reservoir? It got the most votes.
It did, but I rang the centre this morning. They take groups of twenty at most, and there are thirty-six of us. We would have to split the class and go on two different days.
Then that defeats the purpose. What about the escape room in town?
I like it, honestly. But it is twenty-eight dollars each, and Mrs Tan said nobody should pay more than fifteen.
True. Some of us would simply stay at home. All right, the hike up Bukit Timah Hill. It is free.
It is free, and it is also the last week of November. It rains almost every afternoon then. If it pours, we have no back-up, and thirty-six people get soaked.
You sound like my mother. Fine. That leaves the cooking class at the community club.

I thought that one would be boring, but listen. The instructor puts us into teams of six, each team cooks one dish, and then everybody eats lunch together. It is twelve dollars each, including the ingredients.
And it is indoors, so the rain does not matter. Can they take all of us?
Up to forty. The only problem is the date. They are full on the Friday we wanted. They can give us the Thursday instead, from ten until one.
Thursday is fine. The exams end on Wednesday. Do we need to bring anything?
Just an apron and a container, in case there is food left over. Oh, and they need to know by Monday whether anyone cannot eat certain things.
I will make a form tonight and send it to the class chat. You write the plan for Mrs Tan.
Deal. And Wei Jie, put a deadline on the form this time. Last time half the class replied a week late.
Sunday night, nine o'clock. No reply, no lunch.

listening.title: The journey of a library book
listening.intro: You will hear part of a radio programme. A librarian, Mr Rahman, explains what happens to a library book after it is returned. Complete the flow chart and the fact box for questions 1 to 9. Write one or two words or a number for each answer. You will hear the recording twice.

script.text: Most people think that when you drop a book into the returns chute, a librarian picks it up and walks it back to the shelf. Twenty years ago that was true. Today the book goes on quite a journey, and almost nobody sees it.

First, the book slides down the chute onto a moving belt. Every one of our books has a small tag inside the back cover. As the book passes under a reader, the tag is scanned, and in less than a second the book is removed from your account. That is why your phone can show the book as returned before you have even left the building.

Second, the machine checks whether someone else is waiting for the book. If the book has been reserved, the belt pushes it into a red bin, and a member of staff sends it to the right branch that same evening.

If nobody is waiting, the book moves to the third stage, which is sorting. The machine reads the tag again and sends the book into one of twelve bins. There is a bin for children's picture books, a bin for cookery, a bin for Chinese fiction, and so on.

Fourth, each full bin is wheeled to its section by a robot trolley. The trolley follows a line of magnets under the carpet, so it never gets lost, although it does stop politely if a toddler stands in front of it.
Only the last stage still needs a person. A shelver takes the books from the bin and puts each one back in its exact place. We have tried machines for this, but human hands are still faster.

The whole journey takes about forty minutes. Our main branch handles roughly nine thousand books a day this way. And the most common thing we find left inside a returned book? Not money, sadly. It is receipts, usually from the supermarket.

listening.title: A talk about sleep
listening.intro: You will hear a talk about sleep given to a group of Secondary Four students by a school counsellor, Ms Lim. Complete the notes for questions 1 to 8. Write one or two words or a number for each answer. You will hear the recording once only.

script.text: Good afternoon. With the examinations eight weeks away, I want to talk about the one revision tool that costs nothing: sleep.
Let me begin with how much you need. Teenagers need between eight and ten hours a night. A survey of students in this school last year found that the average was only six and a half.

Why does this matter? While you sleep, your brain moves what you learnt during the day into long-term memory. If you cut your sleep short, you cut that process short. Students who stay up to study often remember less the next morning, not more.

So what gets in the way? The first problem is light. The blue light from a phone screen tells your brain that it is still daytime. I recommend putting your phone away one hour before bed, and charging it outside your bedroom, in the living room for example.
The second problem is caffeine. Bubble tea, coffee and energy drinks stay in your body for up to six hours. My advice is no caffeine after three in the afternoon.
The third problem is the weekend. Many of you sleep until noon on Sunday and then cannot fall asleep on Sunday night. Try to get up within one hour of your usual time, even at weekends.
What about naps? A short nap is fine. Keep it under twenty minutes, and take it before four o'clock, or it will steal from your night's sleep.
Finally, if you lie awake worrying, keep a notebook beside your bed. Write the worry down and tell yourself you will deal with it tomorrow. It sounds too simple, but it works for most people.
Sleep is not time taken away from revision. It is part of revision.

oral.title: A beach clean-up
oral.scene: A sunny morning on a sandy beach. About ten people, mostly teenagers in T-shirts and shorts with a few adults behind them, are walking along the shore picking up litter. They wear gloves and carry large clear bags that are already full of rubbish. Three teenagers in front are smiling and laughing as they work. Plastic bottles and wrappers lie on the sand near the water. A large cargo ship is passing close to the shore.
oral.imagePrompt: A realistic photograph of a volunteer beach clean-up on a sunny morning on a tropical sandy beach in Singapore. About ten people of different ages, mostly Asian teenagers in plain coloured T-shirts with a few adults and one older man, pick up plastic litter using tongs and gloves and put it into large rubbish bags. Two teenagers carry a full bag together, smiling. Plastic bottles and wrappers lie along the tide line. Cargo ships far out at sea. Natural light, candid, documentary style, no text, no logos.
oral.planned: Would you take part in an activity like this? Why or why not?
interaction: Some people say that young people today do not care enough about the environment. What is your view?
What can schools do to encourage students to look after public places?
Who should do more to keep Singapore clean: ordinary people or the government? Why?

oral.title: A family meal
oral.scene: A family is sharing dinner at a round table in a busy hawker centre in the evening: a grandfather, a grandmother, a girl and two boys. Plates of food are in the middle of the table. Everyone is leaning in, talking and laughing as they help themselves to the food. Their mobile phones lie in a pile at the edge of the table, untouched. Other tables and food stalls can be seen behind them.
oral.imagePrompt: A realistic photograph of a three-generation Asian family sharing dinner at a round table in a busy Singapore hawker centre in the evening: two grandparents, two parents, a teenage girl and a younger boy. Plates of local food in the middle of the table. Everyone is talking and laughing, the grandmother is serving food onto the boy's plate. A small stack of mobile phones lies untouched at the edge of the table. Warm light, candid, documentary style, no text, no logos.
oral.planned: Would you enjoy a meal like this one? Why or why not?
interaction: How has technology changed the way families spend time together?
Some people think that eating together as a family matters less today than it used to. What do you think?
What can young people do to stay close to the older members of their family?

oral.title: Trying something new
oral.scene: An indoor rock-climbing wall in a sports hall. A girl in a white helmet and a harness is high up on the wall, reaching for the next hold and looking up. Below her, a boy holds her safety rope with one hand and points up to show her where to go. A taller boy beside him is pointing too, and other students stand close by, looking up and calling out to her.
oral.imagePrompt: A realistic wide photograph inside a Singapore secondary school sports hall with a tall indoor rock-climbing wall. A sixteen-year-old Singaporean Chinese girl in a white helmet, a climbing harness and a plain blue T-shirt is high up on the wall, three metres above the floor, reaching for the next hold with a slightly nervous expression, a safety rope running up from her harness. On the floor below, a sixteen-year-old Malay boy holds the other end of her rope with both hands, looking up. Beside him three Singaporean teenagers aged sixteen in plain sports T-shirts and shorts look up and cheer with raised arms. A male instructor points up at a hold. oral.planned: Would you like to try an activity like this? Why or why not?
interaction: Why are some people afraid to try new things?
Should schools make every student take part in outdoor activities? Why or why not?
Is it more important to win or to take part? Explain your view.
